title: The Panama Canal: The Shortcut That Cost a Fortune

beats.text: In 1914, a ship sailing from New York to San Francisco no longer had to fight its way around the stormy tip of South America.
A voyage of about 13,000 miles had suddenly shrunk to roughly 5,200.
The shortcut was a channel about 51 miles long, carved through jungle, rock and swamp.
It cost two nations a fortune. And it cost tens of thousands of workers their lives.
This is the story of the Panama Canal, and of the people who built it.
The dream of a canal across Panama was centuries old. In 1534, King Charles the Fifth of Spain ordered a survey of the isthmus.
In 1881, France made the first serious attempt, led by Ferdinand de Lesseps, the celebrated builder of the Suez Canal.
De Lesseps wanted a canal at sea level, just like Suez, with no locks at all.
But Panama was not a flat Egyptian desert. It was a spine of mountains wrapped in rain forest and soaked by months of tropical rain.
Yellow fever and malaria swept through the work camps. Few people yet understood that mosquitoes carried both diseases.
Landslides buried the diggings almost as fast as the crews could clear them.
By 1889, the French company was bankrupt, and its collapse grew into one of the great scandals of the age.
Historians estimate that about 22,000 workers died during the French years, most of them from disease.
The United States wanted to finish the job. But in 1903, Colombia, which then ruled Panama, rejected the American offer.
On November 3, 1903, Panama declared its independence, and American warships made sure Colombia could not stop it.
Within weeks, a new treaty handed the United States control of a zone about ten miles wide across the isthmus.
Washington paid Panama 10 million dollars, and bought out the French company for 40 million more.
Before the Americans could dig, someone had to keep the workers alive. That job fell to Dr. William Gorgas.
His crews drained swamps, oiled standing water, screened windows and fumigated houses, block by block.
By 1906, yellow fever had been wiped out of the Canal Zone, and malaria was in steady retreat.
Meanwhile, chief engineer John Stevens rebuilt the railroad and persuaded Washington to build a canal with locks.
In 1907, Army engineer George Goethals took command, and he drove the job to the finish.
At the Culebra Cut, steam shovels chewed through nearly eight miles of the Continental Divide, while landslides kept pouring back in.
On the Chagres River, the Gatun Dam created Gatun Lake, the largest artificial lake in the world at the time.
Giant locks, 110 feet wide and 1,000 feet long, would lift ships 85 feet up to the lake and lower them back to the sea.
The locks used no pumps at all. Gravity alone moved millions of gallons of water down from the lake.
On August 15, 1914, the steamship Ancon made the first official passage from ocean to ocean.
The world barely noticed. In Europe, the First World War had just begun.
The American effort cost about 375 million dollars. Official records count roughly 5,600 deaths in the American years.
Much of the hardest labor fell to workers from the Caribbean, many from Barbados, who were paid less and housed apart.
In 1977, President Jimmy Carter and General Omar Torrijos signed treaties to return the canal.
At noon on December 31, 1999, the canal finally belonged to Panama.
In 2016, a new set of larger locks opened, built for the giant ships of a new century.
More than a century later, the shortcut that cost so much still carries ships between the seas every day.
